lines.text: A fault separated your safety capsule from the crew’s ship.
Your crew is still in orbit. Your capsule landed at the old base.
Emergency air and heat are on. The radio is off. Find a way to reach your crew.
A little help can make a big difference.
That’s right! You can use that idea on your next mission.
Try again. Look at the picture, or hear the question once more.
You grew and picked a crop for the crew.
Plants need suitable light, water, nutrients, temperature and air. Our two switches represent only part of that environment.
CSA lists about 21–28 days for leaf lettuce and 45–65 days for soybeans. Our planner used the upper end of each range. Real growing conditions can change the result.
The example soybeans need boiling. Lettuce can be eaten without cooking. Crops add different nutrients to meals, alongside stored food.
A new crop needs cooking. What should the crew include in its plan? A way to prepare the harvest, or Only the planting date?
Your report keeps the measurements and the unanswered questions together.
RAD aboard Curiosity measured radiation on Mars. Our archive shows 84 absorbed dose rate readings, in micrograys per hour, from 1 January 2015.
In a separate 2016 study at Butte M12, surrounding terrain blocked part of the sky. Researchers found a 4% decrease in expected dose rate there.
A missing value means that measurement is unavailable. A reading at one place does not tell us whether another site is safe.
The new site has no radiation reading. What belongs in your report? A measurement is still needed, or The missing reading is zero?
You used stored energy to prepare water for the crew.
Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity. Some spacecraft use sunlight to run their equipment.
A battery stores energy. Spacecraft can use that stored energy when sunlight is unavailable.
An electric motor transfers energy into motion. In our base, the pump uses part of the battery reserve.
When the solar panels are in shadow, what can provide stored energy? The battery, or An empty cable?
Your plan got water ready and a message to the crew.
On Hubble, electricity powers instruments, computers, heaters and transmitters.
Running more devices at once asks for more power. In our base, the pump and radio together exceed the supply limit.
Pausing one job made room for the next. The battery reserve showed how much stored energy remained.
If two jobs exceed the supply limit, what could you try? Run them one after the other, or Switch both on again?
We can reach your crew. First, find the power console with me.
This was a research base. My team left recordings to help explorers like you.
Look through the window. This is a real picture of Mars.
Let’s read a real rover record. Then tell the crew what the evidence shows.
Our base is awake. Next time, we’ll step outside and explore Mars together. This is the end of our demo.
First, connect both radio plugs at the power console.
Tune the antenna until the two signals line up.
The crew can hear us. Send the ready signal.
Open the rover archive. Look for a missing reading.
A dash is not zero. What should we tell the crew?
Repair the relay so the crew can receive your notes.
The crew heard you. The garden is growing. Next time, we step outside.
Your journey log remembers the things you did.
Choose where to go next, or replay the story.
You reached the credits. Thank you for exploring Mars with us.
Start a new journey, or keep the one you saved.
This is a playable demo. The base is imagined, but the rover readings come from Mars.
The crew needs a radio relay and a rover report. Which job will you start with?
Tell the crew what you know. The next site still needs a measurement.
Your notes are ready for the next expedition.
